newsitem.title: GREECE: BANK OF GREECE GOVERNOR SAYS NO LET UP IN MONETARY POLICY.
newsitem.headline: BANK OF GREECE GOVERNOR SAYS NO LET UP IN MONETARY POLICY.

text.p: The Bank of Greece's anti-inflationary monetary and foreign exchange policies will continue but there must be a more effective mix of economic and monetary policies, central bank governor Lucas Papademos told financial weekly 'Ekonomikos Tahydromos'.

"The foreign exchange policies which has been applied in recent years has substantially contributed to the containment of inflationary pressures, despite inflation not responding in the way we wanted, due to the effects of other factors," Papademos said.

"One basic conclusion from economic developments this year - and not only on the inflationary front - is that we need to improve the mix of economic and monetary policies both to deal with inflationary pressures and to create a healthy basis for the medium-term growth of the economy," he said.
This included, he said, a restrained incomes policy which would take into consideration wage developments in competitor countries.
"A basic factor which has burdened inflation are developments in the cost of labour and the cost of production over the last two years," he said.

"Labour costs increased 12 percent in 1994 and 10.5 percent in 1995 and estimates put this year's increase at 9.5 percent. These developments are not in line with the initial forecasted reduction of inflation to 5 percent by the end of 1996".
Papademos said he was certain that the government would continue to apply the Bank of Greece's policy to date, saying it was imperative and gave notice that the 'hard drachma' policy had to continue.

"In regards to foreign exchange policy, the goal for 1996 is to maintain a stable drachma parity with the ECU in the course of the year...By mid-October, the drachma had been devalued slightly against the ECU by one percentage point since the beginning of the year, a development fully consistent with our goals," he said.
Papademos said he was confident that Greece would participate in EMU after 2000 if "the appropriate policies were followed for the next five years".
"The drafting of a credible budget for 1997 in the frameowrk of the Convergence Programme will have a definitive importance on the economy in the next year," Papademos said.

"The basic problem we have is the public deficit. It is the only indicator which is difficult to affect in the next five years," he said, noting, however, a fall in the fiscal debt of five percentage points of GDP over the past two years and the containment of spending on interest.

"The rate of the public debt in relation to GDP, if we follow the right policy, will be controlled. But it is difficult to predict to what degree it will fall at the rate necessary to the forecast target of 60 percent," he said. --Maria Petrakis, Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
